items.t: US Army detonates lead azide stockpile in Iowa despite health and environmental concerns
items.s: The US Army detonated 68 barrels of lead azide at a plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday, as officials offered early assurances while lab results on lead levels were still pending. Residents had raised concerns about possible health and environmental effects.
p: The US Army detonated 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday, according to The Guardian’s live coverage. The Guardian reported that the operation went ahead despite public concern about potential health and environmental effects. A French broadcaster’s report said US officials described the drums as at risk of spontaneous explosion.

The outlets give different figures for the amount of material. The Guardian put it at nearly 9,500 pounds, while the French broadcaster cited some 10,000 pounds of unstable and degraded explosive material. That report also said residents in the area were urged to evacuate amid concerns over possible toxic lead contamination, and that safety measures were being taken to limit contamination from the blast.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has activated an emergency response to support the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, the Guardian reported. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr said that, at President Trump’s direction, his department had deployed personnel to Iowa to help protect families.

Several officials struck a reassuring tone. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin told CNN that he had been told lead levels were very low near the detonation site, and that samples would be sent to a lab as quickly as possible. According to the Associated Press, EPA air monitors did not report any lead in the air during the first 15 minutes after the blast. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said early reports suggested the Army’s mitigation efforts had far exceeded expectations. Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe said initial analysis indicated the explosion was well contained.

Not every reaction was reassuring. Tim Brandt, a resident of Burlington, Iowa, told the Associated Press he had wanted a bigger blast, and said the government had put fear into many people “over nothing.” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker said the state was expected to be minimally affected but remained on alert.

A reporter for KWQC, a CNN affiliate, said he heard a big boom and could see the shockwave as the detonation occurred. The Army has said it will provide an update no later than two hours after the explosion. The EPA said it would continue monitoring during and after the detonation, with post-event sampling and remediation as necessary. Zeldin also encouraged residents to wipe down outdoor surfaces that children touch, such as playsets and railings, with a wet cloth.
items.cav: The quantity of material differs between the two outlets, and the French broadcaster’s summary was cut off, so its details on evacuation advice could not be checked in full. The early claims by Zeldin, Trump and Kehoe about low lead levels and successful containment were not backed by published lab results in the evidence, and Brandt’s view reflects one resident.
items.op: Early reassurances are not the same as measurements. If the Army and EPA want public trust after a blast that prompted evacuation advice, they should publish sample results as they arrive, with methods and locations, rather than asking residents to take officials’ word for it.

items.t: US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, Japan and the EU
items.s: Washington has put forward duties on selected goods from 14 partners, citing industrial overcapacity and unfair trading conduct. The measures would also help make up revenue lost after the Supreme Court rejected earlier tariffs.
p: The US Trade Representative’s office has unveiled proposed duties after an eight-month Section 301 inquiry that examined 16 trading partners, among them Japan, the European Union and South Korea. According to Reuters, as cited by the Guardian, the aim is to curb what the administration describes as “structural excess industrial capacity”.

A senior US official named 14 economies whose goods could face the new charges: China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. Mexico and Norway were also examined, but the USTR has not yet reached findings on either and both sit outside the proposal for the moment.

Officials argue that inexpensive imports from these partners undercut American firms and add to a goods trade deficit that reached $1.24 trillion (€1.13tn) in 2025. The duties would also fill a fiscal gap opened when the Supreme Court ruled in February that the emergency powers statute Trump had relied on did not permit his earlier tariffs.

The proposal rests on a 1974 trade law provision that lets Washington answer foreign conduct judged unreasonable, discriminatory or harmful to US commerce. A senior administration official maintained that the new levies would fit within the trade agreements Trump concluded last year with a large number of countries.

For the EU, the White House is reported to be planning 15% duties on top of existing most-favoured-nation rates, with a possible increase to 20% if ongoing negotiations and prior commitments are deemed inadequate. Certain EU products already hit by Section 232 tariffs, such as vehicles, steel, aluminium, patented drugs and chips, would be spared. The European Commission said it “takes note” of the preliminary finding but firmly disputed that Europe contributes to structural overcapacity.

For China, the USTR proposes rates of up to 20% on many goods, with any Section 301 forced-labour duty subtracted. If talks with Beijing fail to address US concerns, a rate of up to 40% on all Chinese goods could be considered. Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun rejected the overcapacity charges and said “Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone's interest”. An official told AP the measures were unlikely to disturb the US-China trade truce, which expires on 10 January.

Brazil faces separate action after trade discussions made little headway. Washington proposes raising import levies on some sugar and imposing a new 10% charge on completed Brazilian aircraft, a step that would strike Embraer, the country’s largest plane maker.

Comments on the plan are due by 5 January 2027, and hearings are scheduled to start on 25 January. No start date for the duties has been set, and the detailed rates were expected in a Federal Register notice later on announcement day.
items.cav: The sources give different levels of detail on the rates: the Guardian reports a 20% tariff on some Chinese goods stacking to 45% with other duties, while Euronews describes “up to” 20% and a possible 40% if talks fail. The EU figures come from a draft notice, and final rates were not in the evidence. Much of the Guardian’s live blog report relies on Reuters, Bloomberg and the Wall Street Journal, so details are second-hand.
items.op: Tariffs built on a broad investigation, with rates still unpublished and no effective date, leave businesses and trading partners guessing. The public comment period and hearings are the right place to test the evidence of overcapacity. Washington should publish its findings in full, because a trade policy this wide-ranging cannot rest on announcements alone.

items.t: US Army detonates Iowa stockpile of lead azide despite public concern over toxic plumes
items.s: The US Army detonated its entire stockpile of lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant on Wednesday morning, going ahead after several delays and amid worries about health and environmental effects. Officials warned that toxic chemicals could be carried across a wide area.
p: According to The Guardian, the army set off 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the bomb-making chemical at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa with about 400 residents. A reporter for the local station KWQC said a large plume of smoke was visible from more than a mile away.

The explosion risked releasing toxic chemicals across a radius of about 100 miles (160km). The Guardian reported that the likely landing zone shifted as the weather forecast changed. On Tuesday the army published maps projecting that the plume would move south-west of Middletown and then extend into northern Missouri.

The operation had originally been scheduled for the previous Friday but was postponed three times as public concern grew and environmentalists filed a lawsuit to block it. President Donald Trump ordered the military to hold off pending a court ruling and sign-off from Rob Sand, the Democratic governor-elect, who does not take office until January. On Monday, a three-judge panel of the eighth circuit court of appeals ruled that the army could proceed, finding that the Environmental Protection Agency had built adequate safeguards into an emergency permit to limit dust dispersal.

Officials said the material had been found to be dangerously unstable earlier this year and that no “viable alternative” had been identified. Adam Telle, the acting secretary of the army, argued that a controlled detonation was far safer than an uncontrolled one. Josh Turek, the senator-elect, said the chemicals should never have been allowed to degrade and vowed to keep asking how that happened.

The Environmental Protection Agency said it had been on the ground before the blast and would keep monitoring during and after the detonation, with sampling and remediation as needed. The army urged infants, children, pregnant women and people with chronic illnesses to avoid outdoor activities in affected areas until further guidance was issued.

Governor Kim Reynolds issued a disaster emergency proclamation covering Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren counties, and the Iowa National Guard was providing up to 100 soldiers to support safety and outreach. An emergency alert said some people within five miles south-west of the plant could be evacuated, while residents up to 20 miles away were told to stay indoors with windows closed to avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency said it was supporting relocation for all residents of Middletown and nearby areas, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it had activated an emergency response with a multidisciplinary team. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the health secretary, said his department had deployed personnel to Iowa.

The available reporting does not describe the actual outcome of the blast, the extent to which the plume reached populated areas, or any measured health effects. Those findings will matter most for residents, and the monitoring results should be published in full.
items.cav: The source is a single live-updated report and was written before the outcome was known, so it does not confirm what the plume reached or any health effects. Forecast maps and evacuation zones were described as changing, and the claims of officials have not been independently verified.
items.op: A government that stores dangerously unstable material and then asks residents to close their windows owes the public more than reassurance. The court let the detonation proceed, but the real test is whether the EPA’s monitoring data is released quickly, completely and in plain language. Transparency, not official confidence, should decide whether this was worth the risk.

items.t: US Army destroys lead explosives stockpile in Iowa as residents and farmers voice alarm
items.s: Two open-air blasts at an Iowa army site have wiped out a stockpile of lead-heavy munitions, ending a short court fight over fears of toxic fallout.
p: Video showed two successive blasts at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday, starting around 9am local time. The material destroyed was roughly 4,500 kilograms of lead azide, a sensitive explosive that has been part of military ordnance since the First World War.

Before the operation, Governor Kim Reynolds, who is departing office, declared a disaster emergency in three southeastern counties: Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren. The declaration switched on state and county response plans.

Environmental advocates argued that particles could travel far from the site, possibly more than 160 kilometres, and settle on homes, crops and animals. In a video posted on X, Assistant Secretary of the Army Jordan Gillis framed the decision as a choice between an accidental blast and one the military could time and place for public safety.

Updated wind forecasts issued by the Army on Tuesday pointed to lead dust moving toward northeast Missouri. Health authorities there told people living 8 to 32 kilometres southwest of the plant to remain inside, with openings sealed, until they receive word that it is safe.

Local voices have worried that the operation adds pressure to towns already coping with the cost of housing and food and with thin public services. Des Moines County, home to about 38,000 people and including Burlington and Middletown, had 38 percent of households below the ALICE threshold in 2024, according to United for ALICE. Megan Brincks, who chairs the Burlington Homelessness Task Force, said the shelter directive does not stop daily demands on families who need meals, people without homes and those heading to medical visits.

Farming is central to the area, with around 648 farms on nearly 60,300 hectares in the county. The US Department of Agriculture notes that Iowa trails only California in farm output value. USDA undersecretary Richard Fordyce said on Tuesday that roughly 350 farms in Iowa and Missouri may fall within the projected plume zone, an estimate made with the state agriculture department.

Will Sander, a public health academic at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said most of the region’s corn and soybean harvest is already in, which lowers the risk of acute harm to this season’s crops. He urged cattle owners to shield feed and water where they can. Eri Saikawa of Emory University described farmland as the core asset of these families and said damage to it would affect everyone who relies on their crops.
items.cav: The exposure estimates rely on the Army’s revised wind projections and on USDA figures; the article does not report independent measurements of airborne, soil or water lead levels. The farm and plume numbers are estimates, and the reported risk assessments come from outside experts rather than monitoring data.
items.op: Transparency has to be non-negotiable here. Residents and farmers are entitled to independent, published data on wind paths, soil and groundwater before and after any detonation the government frames as the safer option. Shelter orders and disaster declarations are only as credible as the monitoring behind them, and officials should release those results in full.

items.t: Kremlin declines to address reports that up to 700,000 Russian soldiers have died in Ukraine
items.s: The Kremlin declined on Wednesday to comment on reports, built on hacked Russian state statistics, that as many as 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the nearly five-year-long war in Ukraine. Moscow has not published an official military death toll since 2022.
p: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that he would not comment on reports by Russian and international news outlets that around 700,000 soldiers have been killed in the war. He said that only the defence ministry can officially disclose casualty figures and told reporters not to pay attention to other data.

The reports rest on a trove of records taken from the database of Rosstat, Russia’s federal statistics agency. Hackers from two groups opposed to the Kremlin, the Belarusian Cyberpartisans and the pro-Ukrainian Silent Crow, published hundreds of thousands of records earlier this month, according to the outlets’ accounts. The material reportedly covers unpublished causes of death among Russian citizens over the past five years.

Estimates drawn from that data vary. Several international outlets said the figures show confirmed deaths of soldiers close to 500,000. A separate analysis by Meduza and Mediazona, two Russian outlets that are banned in Russia, said that adding soldiers listed as missing, who are widely understood to have been killed but not yet registered, could push the toll as high as 700,000. Some reports put the range at 470,000 to 700,000.

Russia last published a death toll for its army in September 2022, when it said almost 6,000 soldiers had died in the first six months of fighting. That figure has been widely regarded as a significant undercount even at the time.

Moscow has relied on heavy recruitment to sustain the campaign. Reports cited by the outlets say Russia has offered large payments to low-paid workers in poorer regions, recruited men from prisons in exchange for pardons, forcibly drafted more than 300,000 people and recruited thousands from abroad. North Korea has also sent tens of thousands of soldiers to support Russian forces.

Ukrainian losses are also significant, though harder to measure. President Volodymyr Zelensky said in February that about 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers had been killed, a figure thought to be an underestimate. In July, the US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated 125,000 to 150,000 Ukrainian dead, and said about 450,000 Russians had been killed, a figure close to the latest Rosstat-based estimate.
items.cav: The death tolls are estimates built on leaked data and analyses by outside groups, not figures confirmed by either government. The sources give different ranges, and the Kremlin did not dispute or confirm any of them. The hacking claims and the Ukrainian and CSIS figures have not been independently verified in the evidence.
items.op: Civilians and soldiers’ families deserve reliable numbers, and a state that withholds them for years invites doubt. Russia’s refusal to publish a credible toll is not a technicality; it leaves the public to rely on leaks. Transparency about the dead should not depend on a hacker’s data dump.

items.t: Trump proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and EU
items.s: The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that could take effect early next year. The US trade representative’s office announced the plan on Wednesday.
p: The US trade representative’s office said on Wednesday that the administration wants to impose new duties on 14 trading partners, among them China and the European Union, with the measures possibly starting early next year.

According to the office, Beijing would face an extra 20% levy on its goods, lifting the overall charge to roughly 40%. Other economies on the list include Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

The proposal comes after the Supreme Court, in February, found that Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs were unlawful. Its ruling was narrow: it said the administration had misused a particular emergency powers statute, but it did not meaningfully restrict the president’s wider authority to set tariffs.

Officials are now relying on section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, a provision that allows the executive to answer unfair foreign trade practices once formal investigations have been carried out. The White House gave no firm timetable, saying only that the duties could begin in January at the earliest. A hearing is scheduled for 25 January.

This is the second large group of section 301 duties. In July, the White House unveiled levies on more than 80 countries, including Britain, Mexico and Canada, arguing that those nations had not enforced bans on forced labour. Challenges to that earlier package are still waiting for a ruling from the Court of International Trade.

Jamieson Greer, the trade representative, argued in a statement that many partners have built industrial policies around manufacturing targets and labour suppression, which he said skew commerce against America. He framed the plan as a way to make conditions fairer for US workers.

Voters have been sceptical of tariffs, and Democrats took control of Congress in the midterms. The Yale Budget Lab calculates that current tariffs have added $900 in costs per US household. Separately, consumer prices rose at an annualised 3.8% in October, the fastest pace since May and far above the Federal Reserve’s 2% goal.
items.cav: The tariffs are still a proposal, and no final start date has been fixed. The $900 household figure is a Yale Budget Lab estimate, and the claim that seven in 10 Americans blamed tariffs for higher prices comes from an earlier Harris poll, not from this report. The evidence does not show how trading partners have responded.
items.op: Tariffs built on a broad investigative statute should face open hearings, a documented record of unfair practices and real scrutiny in court. Households are already paying more, so Washington owes the public clear evidence before new duties take effect. Transparency is not optional when the costs fall on ordinary shoppers.

items.t: US announces new tariffs on China, the EU and a dozen other trading partners
items.s: The United States has announced a fresh set of tariffs that would hit many of its biggest trading partners, including China and the European Union. The move follows a White House investigation into other countries' trade practices.
p: According to the BBC, the Trump administration has announced new tariffs on imports to the United States, covering China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions. The list includes Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India.

The levies follow an investigation by the White House into the trade practices of other countries, launched in March. That review came after the US Supreme Court ruled that Trump's earlier “Liberation Day” tariffs were illegal.

China faces the highest proposed rate, of up to 40%, while Vietnam faces up to 35%. Other countries face either 20% or 25%. The report notes that some rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs that Trump has agreed to, and that individual countries face different levies.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs would “level the playing field for American workers”. He argued that many trading partners had for decades pursued industrial strategies that distort trade in their favour. These are his claims, and the BBC report does not show independent verification of them.

Economists have warned that tariffs can fuel inflation and push up prices for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, and can also dampen global trade. Trump has argued the policy will boost US manufacturing and create jobs, and he has continued to pursue it despite a poor result for his party in the mid-term elections.

The announcement is likely to add to tensions between Washington and Beijing, which are already locked in a trade dispute. The two countries' tit-for-tat tariff war is currently on hold, and the trade truce is set to expire on 10 January. The BBC reports that no announcement on the truce followed a recent meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping.
The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs and said it will investigate the reasoning behind them. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.
items.cav: The sources do not give effective dates for the new tariffs or explain how the caps apply to each country. Greer's justifications are his own claims, and the Commission's position is reported second-hand through the BBC. The evidence is a single outlet's summary, so details of the White House investigation remain unclear.
items.op: Tariffs imposed after a government review should rest on transparent evidence and clear legal authority, especially after the Supreme Court struck down earlier levies. Shifting, sweeping measures leave businesses and consumers paying for uncertainty. Washington owes its partners a public account of its reasoning.

items.t: Kyiv claims strike damaged five Russian warplanes at Savasleyka base
items.s: Kyiv says it damaged five Russian military aircraft at the Savasleyka airfield east of Moscow and struck two refineries in Russia's Samara region. Neither claim has been independently verified.
p: Kyiv says its forces inflicted damage on five Russian warplanes during a raid on the Savasleyka air base, which lies roughly 185 miles (300 km) east of the Russian capital. The General Staff listed three MiG-31s and two Su-34s among the affected aircraft, but it has not finished measuring the harm. It hinted at further positive developments and did not disclose the munitions involved.

The facility sits in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region and has been under Ukrainian targeting for years. Russia operates aircraft from it that fire hypersonic missiles and glide bombs. When MiG-31s take off, alarms often sound across Ukraine, since their Kinzhal missiles can strike major infrastructure and military sites and are hard to intercept.

Overnight, Kyiv also reported striking two refineries in Samara region, about 500 miles from the front. The attack is the latest in a run of long-distance strikes that have reduced Moscow's oil processing capacity. The defence ministry addressed the plants directly, asking whether they had been repaired and promising another strike if so.
Samara governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev called the night's assault “a true ordeal”, saying more than 145 drones were downed. He reported one fatality and power cuts in several towns.

Kyiv further claimed that a radar installation and fuel and supply depots were hit in Ukrainian areas held by Russian forces. Its ministry contended that vehicles stall without fuel and artillery goes quiet without shells, and that each successful blow reduces the number of strikes Moscow can launch.

On Tuesday, Vladimir Putin urged stronger protection for the nation's energy sites. He maintained that the domestic fuel market had held steady without “critical damage”, and vowed that Moscow would “inevitably” respond against Kyiv. Ukraine, meanwhile, remains under daily attack: ten people died across several regions between 24 and 25 November, and thousands lack electricity after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.
items.cav: The damage figures come from Ukraine's General Staff and have not been independently verified, and the sources do not say what weapons were used. Russia's account of losses at the airfield is not included in the evidence, and the refinery claims rely on Kyiv's statements and Russian regional officials' comments.
items.op: Strikes on military airfields and energy sites carry civilian costs, and claims of success should be checked before they are repeated as fact. Transparent, verifiable reporting from all sides is the only way to judge what is actually being destroyed and who pays for it.

items.t: China flies first foreign astronaut to Tiangong as it widens its space programme
items.s: China has sent Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali to its Tiangong space station, the first foreign astronaut to fly there, as the US-led International Space Station nears the end of its operations. Beijing describes the mission as a step toward broader international space work.
p: Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, is the first Pakistani to reach orbit. Footage showed him drifting through a hatch into the station, where crew members embraced him in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

The Shenzhou 24 capsule lifted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China on Wednesday, with the sky glowing pink at dawn, according to footage. It reached the station and docked roughly three and a half hours later.

Tiangong was completed in 2022 and is the flagship of China’s space effort, which has received large state funding as Beijing tries to close the gap with the United States and Russia. Nasa says the ISS, occupied for 25 years by a five-partner alliance, is set to stop operating in 2030.

President Xi Jinping told his Pakistani counterpart that Beijing was prepared to work with all nations to advance the responsible use of space. Cooperation between the two countries goes back to the early 1990s, and China has previously launched Pakistani satellites. A Pakistani-built rover is also scheduled to travel on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

Ali plans experiments that include growing microalgae as a possible food source and examining how spaceflight affects quinoa seeds. He spent seven months training in Beijing, where he also took demanding Mandarin lessons. Before launch he recited a verse from classical Chinese poetry at a press conference. Commander Tang Hongbo said cultural and linguistic gaps had made joint work harder, but that the effort was worthwhile.

Ali will not serve the six-month stay that Tiangong crews usually complete. He will come home with two members of the Shenzhou 23 crew. Its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay aboard to reach a milestone described as the first full year in orbit by a Chinese astronaut.

Blaine Curcio, of the consultancy Orbital Gateway, told the Guardian that handing a seat to a foreign astronaut on a Chinese-built rocket requires considerable trust from Pakistan. He argued the flight also gives Ali detailed knowledge of China’s crewed programme, which helps Beijing prepare for future missions. Curcio said China seems eager to turn the station into a hub for other countries, pointing to documents it published with the UN describing opportunities for joint work.

The episode sits inside a rivalry. The US has barred China from the ISS since 2011 and prohibits Nasa from collaborating with Beijing, and in 2025 Nasa also blocked Chinese citizens from its facilities. China is aiming to put crews on the moon before 2030, in competition with the US Artemis programme. Curcio suggested Brazil and Egypt might seek places on Chinese flights, and that if no Western successor to the ISS appears, Russia or other ISS partners could eventually fly to Tiangong. These remain his forecasts.
items.cav: The available evidence is one detailed report and a short BBC summary, which says only that Ali is the first foreign national to board Tiangong. Predictions about Brazil, Egypt and other countries are one analyst’s speculation, not announced plans.
items.op: Space is a shared domain, and each new partnership should be judged by its openness. Pakistan’s trust in a Chinese rocket is a serious choice, and the public deserves clear information on crew safety, terms and the purpose of the work. Cooperation that stays opaque will not earn that trust.

items.t: Overnight drone barrage kills at least seven in Ukraine as Ukrainian drones reportedly hit Russian refineries
items.s: Russian drones struck energy and civilian sites across Ukraine overnight, leaving at least seven dead in six regions. Ukrainian drones reportedly hit three Russian oil refineries in the same period.
p: Overnight on Wednesday, Russia sent a large swarm of drones at energy and civilian sites across Ukraine. Local officials put the death toll at no fewer than seven across six regions. Ukraine’s air force said it counted 112 drones of the Shahed, Gerbera and Parodiya types, and that 88 were downed or disabled.

In Bila Tserkva, in Kyiv region, one person died after a blast hit critical infrastructure, an Epicentr shopping centre and a Nova Poshta branch, local authorities reported. In Kharkiv region, a strike on a minibus on a highway killed one person and injured seven, according to governor Oleh Synehubov. In Sumy region, a 76-year-old and a 69-year-old were killed, and a third person was hurt.
Attacks on Tuesday evening killed a 41-year-old and a 17-year-old in Odesa region, and one person died and three were hurt in Zhytomyr region. Chernihiv and Donetsk regions also reported casualties.

Energy assets took much of the damage. Serhiy Fedorenko, acting head of Naftogaz, said a gas production site in Poltava region was hit, sparking a fire and halting output. He called it a repeated attack and accused Moscow of targeting gas production so Ukrainians would be left without heat in winter. Facilities in Dnipropetrovsk region were also struck, forcing emergency outages. Officials reported major losses of power in Zaporizhzhia region, and more than 9,000 customers in Odesa region were left without electricity.

DTEK said one of its thermal power plants took a large strike that caused serious damage and forced it offline. The company did not disclose the location, but said this was the third such strike on its plants in November.

Inside Russia, Ukrainian monitoring sources said drones hit three refineries overnight. Two plants in Samara region, Kuibyshev and Syzran, both owned by Rosneft, caught fire. Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed an attack without naming the sites, and said one person died and some districts lost power. He also reported 145 drones downed over the region, a claim Euronews said it could not verify. In Rostov region, governor Yuri Slyusar confirmed an attack on the Novoshakhtinsk refinery, which halted operations after a strike involving more than 50 drones and missiles lasted six hours.

Ukraine’s General Staff said it hit the Savasleyka airbase in Nizhny Novgorod region, a major aviation site it linked to Kinzhal missile launches. It claimed three MiG-31 and two Su-34 aircraft were damaged. Last week, Ukraine also destroyed part of a road span of the Crimean Bridge, stopping car traffic, while trains have resumed.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy presented the deep strikes as a reply to Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, calling them “long-range sanctions”. He had earlier said Kyiv would stop hitting Russian refineries only if Moscow ended its attacks on Ukraine’s energy system. On Tuesday, Vladimir Putin threatened retaliation over the refinery strikes and faulted Kyiv for ignoring calls from Donald Trump to halt attacks on oil processing sites.
items.cav: The refinery damage comes from Ukrainian monitoring sources, and Russian officials did not name all the facilities, so the scale of the damage is not independently confirmed. The 145-drone claim for Samara region could not be verified. Casualty figures come from local authorities and may rise.
items.op: Civilian deaths and winter heating cuts should not become bargaining chips for either side. Whatever the military logic of refinery strikes, both capitals owe their citizens a clear account of targets and casualties. Vague talk of sanctions and retaliation tells readers little about who is being protected.

items.t: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after Trump says he pressed the board
items.s: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, a little more than a week after he resigned amid reports of extramarital affairs. Its shares jumped more than 33 percent on the news.
p: Nvidia’s board has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive, reversing his resignation earlier this month. The chipmaker announced the move on Monday, and the company said the decision took effect immediately.

Huang stepped down after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman whom US intelligence is said to believe is a Chinese spy. Al Jazeera described the affairs as at least two in number and said the alleged spy was a suspected Chinese agent. Those claims are not confirmed in the sources.

President Donald Trump said on CNBC that he had spoken with the board “directly and indirectly” and had convinced its members to bring Huang back. He said the board had asked for assurances on national security risks and that his administration had provided them. Trump also said he had spoken with Huang on Sunday night, before the announcement.

Nvidia said its leadership had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk. Trump wrote on Truth Social that the government had no reason to believe the return posed any risk. The sources do not publish the assurances themselves, so their content can only be judged from these official statements.

The return followed a campaign by Elon Musk and others. A petition calling for Huang’s return drew more than 180,000 signatures within days of his departure, according to Al Jazeera. Musk posted that “the mistake has been corrected” after the announcement. Colette Kress, who had served as interim CEO, will remain chief financial officer.

Analysts said Huang’s role at Nvidia is central to the wider spending boom in data centres and chips. BBC News reported that the company sells chips to customers including Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, and has also provided funding to firms in its supply chain, a practice known as circular financing. Some investors worry that a pullback in Nvidia’s spending could spread to the wider US economy. Dan Ives said Nvidia could have lost as much as 30 percent of its value without Huang, a view Al Jazeera attributed to him.

Several issues remain open. Al Jazeera reported that investigations into the company by the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the Department of Justice are still ongoing. Goldman Sachs, cited by the BBC, expects investment in this spending wave to exceed $1 trillion in 2026. Early trading on Monday showed strong gains across major US indices, with the Nasdaq up 6.7 percent.
items.cav: The alleged spy link and the number of affairs are reported claims, not established facts, and the assurances given to the board have not been published. The sources also differ slightly on the share jump, with one saying more than 33 percent and another 33 percent.
items.op: A chipmaker’s leadership should not be settled by a president’s phone calls and national-security assurances the sources do not publish. Whatever the merits of Huang’s return, investors and citizens are being asked to trust private briefings while federal inquiries remain open. Transparency about what was promised, and to whom, should come before the market celebrates.

items.t: Trump backs Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as lawmakers press national security questions
items.s: US President Donald Trump has said he spoke with Nvidia’s board about Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive and that the company’s concerns over national security were addressed. House committees say the reinstatement “changes nothing” for their own inquiry.
p: Donald Trump told CNBC that he had spoken “directly and indirectly” with Nvidia’s board about the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive, which he described as the correct decision. In a phone interview, Trump said he had also spoken with Huang the night before the board announced the move.

According to Trump, the board asked for assurances on national security risks, and the administration provided them. He said the government had conducted a “very thorough investigation” into Huang and concluded that Huang had shown bad judgement in somewhat unrelated incidents but had done nothing wrong. Trump said Huang had been exonerated. The evidence does not include the findings of that investigation, and Trump’s account is his own.
Trump also declined to say whether he had joined the Nvidia board meeting, saying only that he “was represented at the board”.

A spokesperson for the House intelligence committee told NBC News that the reinstatement changes nothing for three House committees, which plan a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on 1 December. Nvidia’s general counsel is due to appear the following day. The committee spokesperson said serious questions about national security implications still need answers.

Senator Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate intelligence committee, said the decision showed that national security was “up for sale”. Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to chair the Senate banking committee from January, called the decision “reckless” and said the board still owes Congress answers about the company’s compliance with US export controls.

The reinstatement follows reports, cited by the New York Times, that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had been in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 until this autumn. The Times reported this on the basis of people with knowledge of US intelligence reports, and the claims have not been confirmed in the evidence.

Markets responded strongly. Nvidia’s shares were reported to have risen by about 31 per cent at the start of trading, while the S&P 500 jumped 4.5 per cent. Reports on the size of the share gain vary, with one headline citing 33 per cent.
items.cav: The sources do not establish whether Huang was cleared of wrongdoing; that claim comes from Trump. The Alice Huang reports are second-hand, cited from the New York Times, which is behind a paywall. The share increase is reported inconsistently, as 31 per cent in one part of the coverage and 33 per cent in another.
items.op: A chief executive’s return matters to the public when it touches export controls and national security. When a president vouches for a company’s leader while Congress is still seeking answers, the public deserves the same transparency. The assurances given to the board should be disclosed, not left for closed-door sessions.

items.t: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he resigned
items.s: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive, less than two weeks after he resigned. Its board said it had received input from senior US government levels before making the decision.
p: Nvidia’s board of directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, according to a company statement. The board said it was satisfied with “Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia” after a series of discussions and meetings.

The board said that, based on input from senior levels of the US government, it was confident Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk. It did not name the officials involved or describe the input in detail.
President Donald Trump praised Huang as a “great patriot and national treasure”. The Guardian’s live blog reported that Trump said he had spoken to the Nvidia board directly about Huang.

Colette Kress, who had served as interim CEO while keeping her role as chief financial officer, was thanked by the board for her service. The live blog’s headline said Nvidia shares rose 33% on the news, adding $1tn to the company’s value.
items.cav: The sources do not explain why Huang resigned. The government input is unnamed, and the 33% gain and $1tn figure appear only in the live-blog headline, so they are not confirmed in the excerpt.
items.op: A company’s leadership decision shaped by unnamed government input deserves more openness than a one-line assurance. Markets and the public should be told what officials said and why it satisfied the board. Without that, a national security clearance looks like a private deal.

items.t: Hacked Russian records point to more than 1,000 military suicides in the Ukraine war
items.s: Russian state records, obtained in leaked form and analysed by the Guardian, list more than a thousand soldiers as having taken their own lives since the invasion began. The newspaper and its sources believe the true total is higher.
p: The Guardian’s analysis of a cache of more than 11 million death certificates puts the number of Russian soldiers recorded as suicides since the full-scale invasion at over 1,000. The paper says that total roughly equals one regiment. The figures are drawn from records held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics body, which has not made them public.

The newspaper illustrates the pattern with one man, Alexei Bolgov, a sergeant guarding a headquarters in occupied Donetsk. In late 2024 he reportedly told his wife by phone that what he was witnessing was dreadful and promised to explain when he returned. According to a written account by his commander, which the Guardian has seen, he walked roughly 300 metres from his unit’s post into woodland about five weeks later and shot himself, shortly after his 29th birthday. “On the day of his death, Bolgov was in a withdrawn state,” the commander wrote.

A separate group of 885 deaths in or near Ukraine was logged as firearm-related injuries of “undetermined intent”. Specialists warn that this label can hide suicides, and the Guardian says it independently confirmed several such cases as suicides. Taken together with the confirmed suicides, the paper counts 1,038 similar deaths, 885 of them in or near Ukraine.

Of the 1,087 suicides the paper has identified, at least 614 occurred in occupied Ukrainian territory or in the Russian border regions of Belgorod and Bryansk, while 113 entries give no location. More than half involved firearms, often near the front, at camps, training grounds and private homes. The wartime cases include 43 soldiers aged 18 or 19. The wider set also contains 108 men under 25 who died by suicide elsewhere in Russia, some of whom may have been conscripts pressed into contracts.

Recorded cases rose from more than 50 in 2022 to more than 200 in 2024, reaching a peak of 365 in 2025. The database already holds almost 300 suicides for 2026, which the paper describes as the second-highest yearly total of the war so far. It stresses that the records are incomplete and lag behind events at the front.

Analysts cited by the Guardian point to pressure from commanders and fellow soldiers, dread of lethal assignments, and contracts that offer little or no way out. Rob Lee of the Foreign Policy Research Institute described coercion by the military, including abuse and torture, and said it was unsurprising that some men take their own lives. Ivan Chuvilyaev, a spokesperson for Idite Lesom, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert, called the official count an underestimate: “I would say it is a low estimate.” He also argued that many self-inflicted deaths on the battlefield are probably logged as combat losses.

The Kremlin does not publish military suicide data and treats casualty figures as a state secret. The Guardian also examined the case of Sergei Savenok, a lieutenant colonel from the Irkutsk region who was found shot dead in occupied Luhansk in July 2023. Officials told his wife that he had died by suicide, yet he does not appear in the Rosstat suicide records. A certificate matching his date of birth instead records an injury from a handheld firearm of undetermined intent.
items.cav: The figures come from a hacked cache of death certificates and the Guardian’s own analysis, not from an official Russian publication, and the sources provided do not include a Kremlin response. The claims that the true number is higher are estimates from experts and activists, not measured totals, and the case details rely on a commander’s account and a wife’s report.
items.op: When a state hides its war dead, families and the public are left to rely on leaks and hacked files. Counting how soldiers die is basic accountability, not wartime propaganda. Until Moscow publishes its records, its silence should be read as a choice, and it deserves to be challenged.
